items.title: 4.2 Relationship between mole, molar mass and Avogadro's number

source_refs.note: Topic 4.2, printed pages 76-78; Sample Problems 4.4 to 4.6 and Quick Check 4.2 as the self-check. Sample 4.5's '0.602 x 10^23' is given as 6.02 x 10^22.

blocks.text: A sample of 12.0 g of natural carbon contains the same number of atoms as 4.0 g of natural helium: both contain one mole of atoms, 6.02 x 10^23. Different masses of elements have the same number of atoms: 1.0 g of hydrogen, 23.0 g of sodium and 238.0 g of uranium are each one mole, 6.02 x 10^23 atoms. An atom of sodium is 23 times heavier than an atom of hydrogen, so to have equal numbers of atoms sodium must be taken 23 times greater in mass. Likewise 18.0 g of water and 180.0 g of glucose are each one mole, 6.02 x 10^23 molecules: one mole of different compounds has different masses but the same number of molecules. The number of ions in one mole of different ionic species is also always Avogadro's number: 96.1 g of sulfate ions and 62.0 g of nitrate ions are each 6.02 x 10^23 ions.

The number of moles can be found by dividing the number of particles by Avogadro's number: n = N / NA. Putting the relationships together, number of particles = (mass of substance x NA) / molar mass. Mass in grams divided by molar mass gives moles, and moles multiplied by Avogadro's number gives the number of particles.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: Juglone, a dye from the husks of black walnuts, is a natural herbicide: it kills competing plants around the tree but not grass. Isopentyl acetate, C7H14O2, gives bananas their scent, and a bee releases about 1 x 10^-6 g of it when it stings, which draws other bees to attack.
